=== POST ===
So far he is managing but there are signs of the beginning of decline: needs help with bills, rotting food in fridge, more forgetfulness. I know we need to find out what health/medicaid plans he has so we know what services will be covered.I guess I am asking for advice on what else we could be doing now - for anyone that has gone through this was there something you realized or found out later you wish you had done sooner?

=== COMMENT 1 (2026-06-02T11:48:50.527-0400) ===
Just wanted to add a little cautionary note here, from learning the hard way. If your dad still insists upon carrying his wallet as mine does:

First, if he will let you hold all his cards, IDs, etc that would be in his wallet—that is preferable. I use a wallet with two sections—one for me and one for my dad. We also take pics of each front and back in case of loss.

My dad carries a small bit of cash in his wallet and that is all now. You can purchase wallets on Amazon that contain a little sleeve for an air tag. That way when the wallet is misplaced, it is easier to locate it. 

(I won’t bore you with the details of the weekend totally consumed when we all thought he had lost his wallet still full of cards and IDs—searching a parking lot and inquiring at businesses, freezing credit, reporting stolen/lost cards, social security, etc etc etc. Ultimately found in an obscure place at home a week later, thankfully! )

=== COMMENT 2 (2026-05-30T22:26:33.280-0400) ===
Make sure all needed legal documents are in place, POA for healthcare and financial, advance directive, and will. The POA for finances should now take over his finances, paying bills and watching out for any signs of financial abuse, such as being taken advantage of by scammers, relatives, friends, or charities. Have him seen by his doctor for a complete evaluation, letting the doctor know your concerns ahead of the visit. Don’t be afraid to act, don’t hesitate to do what’s best out of fearing his reaction, don’t let a person with probable dementia drive the bus on decisions. It often feels like an awkward place to be with a person you’ve been conditioned to respect and obey, but it’s a new place now, accept this. I wish you both peace

=== COMMENT 3 (2026-05-30T19:29:55.757-0400) ===
Make sure you have a list of every asset, every bank account, every health care provider along with logins if online.

=== COMMENT 4 (2026-05-30T12:13:25.200-0400) ===
I totally sympathize with your situation. But - he isn't managing! And this is not the beginning of decline. He's past the beginning.

Needs help with bills - no way a normal person would let bills slide if he's been handling them well during his adult life.
Rotting food in fridge - way beyond beginning. A normal person would be getting rotting food out as soon as there's a need to remove it. Executive function kicks in and says "Oh, that fruit has been in there for xx weeks, time to take a look and make sure none of it is rotting." Cognitively declining person losing executive function says, "What fruit? There's no fruit."
Forgetfulness - if he doesn't live with you, you aren't aware of everything he's forgetting. 

He shouldn't be living alone, but don't move him into your house! He needs 24/7 supervision, not just a sitter for 4 hours a day. You've very wise to want to get ahead of this, and the time is now. Take a look at continuing care facilities. He can start at one level and continue through the levels as his condition declines. also, he can make friends and won't be lonely. Also, if he'shard of hearing, get him hearing aids. Loss of hearing contributes to cognitive decline in a big way.

Good luck with what you need to do.

=== COMMENT 5 (2026-05-30T11:37:18.207-0400) ===
Well because it is me answering....
Is your dad a Veteran? If so get whatever info you can and contact your local Veteran's Assistance Commission. Their service is free and they will help find out if he qualifies for any benefits. It does not matter if he served during war time he is still a Veteran. The type of benefits will vary depending on where and when he served. It could be a little or a LOT. Well worth checking out. And don't let him tell you there are "others that need it more" his benefits are HIS and by taking his benefits he is NOT causing someone else to lose theirs. (big concern for many Vet's)

Next check with your local Senior Service Center or Area Agency on Aging. There may be programs that can help him.

Is there an Adult Day Program near? If so that can help a lot. Typically they pick you the participant in the morning, provide a breakfast, lunch and a snack. A variety of activities and then bring them home late in the afternoon. 

See an Elder Care Attorney. He may still be cognizant enough that he can appoint a POA for Health and Finances. if not someone may have to become his Guardian. So if he has a "good" time of day make the appointment for then. 
If there is any possibility that he may have to apply for Medicaid find out how that can be done legally. (there is a "5 year look back" so no gifting or "hiding" money)

Ask him what his wishes are for Health care. A document that is more detailed than a DNR is a POLST (called by other names in some States) it goes into detail about what measures he would want taken. 
Pre paying, preplanning his funeral is one way to spend down assets and take a huge burden off the families shoulders when he does die. 

figure out the Where will he go. 
Will he move in with a family member? 
will a family member move in with him? 
Will he go to a facility that can care for him safely? 
Will he stay in his home with a caregiver?

=== COMMENT 6 (2026-05-30T11:20:50.043-0400) ===
Wow have I been there (and still am almost six years later). It’s time to have a conversation about the fact that “none of us are getting any younger”, and you think it would be a good idea to get with an attorney (an elder care attorney, but you don’t have to present it that way), so that everyone’s wishes and expectations are clear for the future. You can even let him know you were just reading about this (true), and it is a really good idea.

The attorney can help him establish all the paperwork to make sure his health wishes are respected (like does he want a DNR, does he want to have certain life saving measures attempted or not. —like ventilators, etc.), he can elect a POA in case he is ever deemed incapable, etc. It doesn’t mean death or dementia is imminent, it is just so all ducks are in a row and everyone knows his wishes. It’s good for everyone. He can also do a will or trust, etc to take care of his finances.

Everything that has to be done is a lot to digest and can be emotional and feel to him like loss of independence and privacy. But it is really to protect him and make sure his wishes are known and respected. At this point (my dad had a cancer diagnosis so it made broaching the subject easier), my dad took me to all his doctors appointments (I had already been driving him to them, just not attending them), and signed HIPPA forms allowing the doctors to talk to me, make appointments for him, etc. If you are going to be that person in his life, then be prepared. Depending on his current and future health issues, this alone can be a lot of time, effort, and emotion coordinating between specialists and researching appropriate [member], etc., scheduling labs and following up on them (doctors don’t look at them until you broach the subject or have an appointment, so if there is something that needs quick attention you have to instigate it), etc. My dad just turned that all over to me. Because of his poor hearing he had barriers to communication (especially since it was still covid times and everyone was masked). Your dad may not want that level of involvement from you so you will have to navigate with respect all of that.

The attorney can also discuss with him daily finances and having backup help there .

It sounds like he could use some help with daily life. I was seeing what you are seeing, after my mom died and my dad was trying it out on his own at his house. I also observed a lot of dropped meds on the floor and poor hygiene (dad also has vision issues). It was “easy” for me to broach him having help, because of his cancer diagnosis. It may be less well received by your dad. Mine moved in with us (NOT something I would recommend, but my relationship dynamic and situation may be different from yours, and it was still very much Covid when we were addressing all this). There are various ways to arrange and pay for care help in the home, or he could consider Assisted Living apartments. You will get a lot of good advice here. I would recommend always treating him with respect and consideration and LISTEN to him. I would very carefully consider how involved you become in daily care and what you are and are not willing to do—reading on this site some of the issues and situations that can come up that you would not be able to anticipate yourself, and carefully weighing options.

Adding to my already very long response: [member] very wisely suggested taking him to his PCP to check out possible reasons why you are seeing what you are seeing in his home. Elderly do not present with the usual UTI symptoms, always, and I have found some docs are less familiar with that fact and that the bigger symptoms can be cognitive, fatigue, etc. Some vitamin deficiencies definitely can effect daily functioning, etc!

=== COMMENT 7 (2026-05-30T10:41:07.233-0400) ===
If you are seeing these symptoms on a regular/daily basis he is probably already in moderate level of impairment, not the beginning. If it is dementia, it starts little by little over the course of years (usually). By time it manifests itself obviously he is well into it. 

As suggested by [member], make sure he has all his legal ducks in a row so that he has all protections in place and documents that will make managing his affairs legal and efficient. 

Next, take him in for a full medical exam to make sure that what you're seeing is actually some form of dementia and not a treatable problem, like a UTI, dehydration, vitamin deficiency, uncontrolled diabetes, high blood pressure, strokes/TIAs, tumor, etc. Only a few dementias can be diagnosed through imaging. Start with his PCP. Make sure you or a male family member accompanies him to this appointment and is in the exam room with him ("to take notes because the doctors tell you lots of stuff and talk fast"). Make sure he assigns someone as his Medical Representative on the HIPAA form that all medical offices have. This does not permit medical decisions for him, but legally allows his medical team to discuss and receive his private medical information without further permision or need to be present. 

Once you know what's going on, you will need to figure out if he's safe staying by himself in his home or if he needs in-home aids or a move to an AL. At the end of day you can't force a resistant adult to do/accept things they fight against, but this is where having durable PoA becomes critical.

=== COMMENT 8 (2026-05-30T10:24:55.527-0400) ===
The first thing I would do is get access to your father's financial and health-care information. Find out whether he has power-of-attorney documents. If he doesn't, ask him to get them ASAP. You might need to nag, encourage, or help him with getting the documents. This is common. Many folks don't like to think about or prepare for their own decline and death. Persist through any hesitation on his part. Good luck!

Before  I vent here yet again in the support group, I know, I know I've been a member here for many years. Bear with me. I have taken much advice from many wise and knowledgeable women on this site and at times this has been my only unbiased support group I could count on.That being said I'm doing my best not to implode from the stress that is going on with having my Mom placed in long term care. I've traded not being able to care for her alone to selling her house to self pay until that runs out and Medicaid is sought. Me being the fiduary as her POA. I have probably suffered from some form of depression for years and having to deal with real estate contracts and even the process of dealing with the administrative parts of the front office at the facility to go ahead and apply for Medicaid. I feel like I'm being plucked to death from one end to the other. So, I have been docu signing and hand written signatures so much lately my head is spinning.Not to mention contracts falling through with the selling of the house and disappointment after disappointment.I am contacting yet another avenue to help me with all of the legal aspects of managing what I have been trying to do for years. Covering my assets. An Elder Law Attorney. What that means to me is having to stretch my mental health to understand what is happening with dear Mom. I haven't visited with her in over a week. I am seeing a therapist and she is helping me navigate some of this. In the long run, I'm just not seeing the rewards of doing all of this for someone who has manipulated me and verbally abused me in the past, etc., etc. and pretend how much I love her for just being Mom. All the times of her saying this house will be mine one day! If I am repeating that same point, I apologize. I have recently lost a close friend of mine and haven't had time to really mourn her. I just want to go away for a few days even by myself and chill and shut some of this out. I'm not exactly green to dealing with lawyers and even real estate agents but it all stems back to 'saving the house' and it's crazy letting an inanimate thing make you crazy. Doing the same thing and expecting different results, right.Not sure what I'm asking here, if anything. I just need to know I'm doing the right thing and hopefully one day I can put this behind me because I know she will probably outlive me. Even then that might be the only peace of mind I ever get. And no I'm not going to harm myself. Thank you again for reading from an old member of Agingcare. I hate sounding like a defeatist or victim. Ughhh

=== COMMENT 2 (2026-09-08T17:42:09.000-0400) ===
Yay for great progress! The house is sold and mom has Medicaid. Those are huge positive steps. Good for you! 
Seems someone wants to treat, maybe fix, long term depression. I’d view a fix as a long shot, but what’s to lose by treatment? You don’t have to be involved. It will either prove she’s amendable or not amendable to treatment, not your issues either way. She’s in a facility, she’s safe, you’re not providing any hands on care. You visit on your terms, your schedule, you leave anytime it’s too much. Remember that! Take care of you, rest and heal. Wishing you much peace

The bottom line is that caregivers need caring for. Until society stops focusing on the nice-teethed seniors dressed in pearls and fine cashmere sweaters, then only will we get to the the meat and bones of the difficulties caregivers face every minute of the day. 

Recognition and tangible help is king. 

Its about dam* time there was caring for the caregiver, without first emptying their bank accounts or forcing them into a mental institution.

=== COMMENT 9 (2026-08-08T08:53:21.000-0400) ===
@[member]

I have to compliment you on your very honest response here. You nailed it. 
Too true that we've all seen the AARP propaganda featuring the gorgeous, grey-haired seniors with the perfect teeth. My personal favorite was the AARP edition with Harrison Ford right around the release of the 'Yellowstone 1923' prequel still being able to jump up on a horse. The caption was something along the lines of that being what 78 looks like. In what universe is Harrison Ford, Liam Neeson, or Mick Jagger your garden-variety elder? In no universe LOL. These guys will pay for their own care if they ever need it and not put it on their families. The other was Bruce Willis who has FTD. His wife simply had a house built for him on their estate where a round-the-clock staff of professionals take care of him 24/7. Her and the children visit him. Not the same as being the sole caregiver for a LO with FTD that you have to take care of 24/7 on your own. Not the same at all. Gotta love AARP propaganda.

=== COMMENT 10 (2026-08-04T18:02:31.000-0400) ===
The myth of how rewarding it is to be a caregiver comes from misguided AARP propaganda, TV commercials where people with expensive teeth smile and smile and smile at attractive gray-haired elders, and ads where old people are encouraged to come for a wine tasting at a castle in their town where they will get a free month's rent if they sign up before whenever. Happy, happy, happy all the time! and there are never any pix of dirty diapers, or panicky conversations about how we're going to get mom to her doctor appointment when she refuses to get in the car, or picking dad up from his 35th fall this month when you threw your back out picking him up last Thursday. So let's declare the truth: CAREGIVING IS NOT REWARDING. We do it because we love them (or maybe we hate them but they make us do it by promising their house) or because we can't figure any way out of it. Plus all families are not happy, all caregivers are not perfect, and we've been duped. The myths have caused depression and anxiety for lots of family caregivers. We feel that we have to live up to the cheery expectations. Speak up, speak out, and tell the truth. That's what I am doing right now.

=== COMMENT 11 (2026-08-04T14:29:33.000-0400) ===
It's easy to become overwhelmed and even depressed after years of caring for an elder parent, or anyone - in my case, it's my husband. I experienced a period of depression at about the 5 year mark, which I think contributed to my physical breakdown. 
I'm glad you are seeing a therapist, and I hope that is ultimately helpful for you.
Something you said, that you're just not seeing the reward of doing all of this. 
I don't think there is any reward. Sometimes it's just what needs to be done. If it is more than you can manage, can you possibly step away and delegate more to a professional? Are you trying to "save the house" so you have that asset after your mother passes? Do you need it? If you walked away right now, go back to living your own life for you, do you have sufficient income, assets, home, support network of friends? Have you considered relinquishing your POA and have the court assign a guardian for your mom?
Go ahead and get away from everything for a few days, shut off your brain, mourn your friend. Let the realtor and the attorney do as much as they can without bothering you.

=== COMMENT 12 (2026-08-04T09:15:29.000-0400) ===
There are no rewards. Even for people who are homecare workers. When the word "rewarding" is used in employment it usually translates into 'low-paying, hard, crappy work where you (the worker) will be treated badly'. When "rewarding" is a term used for becoming a family caregiver to a needy, elderly LO that translates into 'you're going to be an unappreciated, unpaid, stressed out care slave who will be treated badly'. Beware of the word "rewarding".

You're doing the right thing and moving forward. Take some time for yourself and try to remember that everything you've done and are currently doing for your mother is done out of love. 

Seeing an elder law attorney is a really good idea. One that has a backround in estate planning though. That's important. It's totally understandable you not wanting to lose your mother's house. Don't let anyone tell you differently. If the house has to go to pay for your mother's care, you will deal with it.

Your mother is in a care facility now and that takes a huge burden off of you. One day at a time, my friend. You will be okay.

=== COMMENT 13 (2026-08-02T11:01:30.000-0400) ===

There are no rewards in caregiving. It is just a long hard slog.

You will get through this and it will be ok.

=== COMMENT 15 (2026-08-01T13:52:48.000-0400) ===
You're definitely doing the right thing but there ARE no "rewards" involved, only anxiety (imo). Mother's like ours weren't able or willing to give us "peace of mind". Ever. Only worries and fears that no matter how much we did for them, it was never enough. They made and make us feel very small. I felt defeated my whole life when it came to my mother. With others, I was confident and capable. It was only my mother who had the ability to reduce me down to feeling like garbage. 

Take this monumental task in very small bites. Stop to rest and regroup. Take that vacation. Mother is where she belongs, cared for by others and safe. You are free to go away if you'd like. 

I always said what you said.....my mother is going to outlive me. She recovered from pneumonia 3x, it was like she was invincible. On earth just to persecute me. One day I got a call from the hospice nurse that she'd had "a status change". Meaning she went to bed and was in a semi comatose state, not eating or drinking, etc. I didn't believe it and went to the Memory Care to see for myself. It was true, she was at end of life, at 95+. She died exactly 1 week later. I felt relieved tbh. 

Just do what you need to do at your own pace. Hire help. Don't let this kill YOU. You've been a fine daughter to a mother who didn't deserve such devotion. And when she dies, you'll know you did everything in your power to help her live her best life possible. For no reward and for no thanks. Just because it's your nature to be a good person. And you'll feel peace in your heart as a result. 

One day at a time, my friend. This too will end.

=== COMMENT 16 (2026-08-01T13:34:18.000-0400) ===

=== COMMENT 17 (2026-08-01T12:16:28.000-0400) ===
I overwhelm easily so I end up taking things one at a time. 

If Mom does not or will not have enough money for her care in LTC, then you need to apply for Medicaid. In my State you should do this 60 to 90 days before the money runs out. I started in mid April with the application. The caseworker gave me a list of things he needed to complete the application. Mom had 20k left. I placed her in LTC on May 1st. Her 20k paid for May and June. By June I had emailed everything needed for the application to the caseworker. I confirmed this with him. July 1st Medicaid started. 

Yes, my Mom had a house that was up for sale. It must be sold at Market rate to satisfy Medicaid. If sold while she is on Medicaid, Medicaid stops, your spend down the house proceeds and then go back on Medicaid. Once my Mom was on Medicaid, I stopped paying her taxes, they are high where I live. I unplugged all her appliances. Had one light that came on at dark and went off at 11. I set her heat at 55. I was paying those bills so tried to keep them low. My Moms house did not sell while she was alive. Since she was only on Medicaid for 3 months, she owed them 6k so a lien was placed. With that lien the tax and water liens on the house, I was able to sell it for what I could get as long as I covered the liens which I did. The bills that I paid were reimbursed at the house closing.

You are not responsible to pay anything towards your mothers care. Her house, the realtor is handling the sale. Now, you clean it out, one room at a time. I stared by cleaning out trash first. Each room had 3 piles....keep, throw out and give away. Give away went to thrift shops and friends if they wanted something. I did tackle the kitchen first because of the food. 

You have to prioritize. I had a disabled nephew who lived with Mom. He could fend for himself so I was able to put him on the back burner while I concentated on Mom. It has to be done so you just keep going. When its all done it feels so good.

=== COMMENT 18 (2026-08-01T10:46:49.000-0400) ===
I agree with [member].
My mom died about 10 days ago. I was not close to her, but I did my duty over the years, especially in the past three years or so; I would visit her and my sister (closest in geography and emotionally to mom) almost every week.
I didn't have nearly as much work to do for my mom, either while she was alive or since her death, as you have for yours, and still I am exhausted. 
I encourage you to get away for a little while. So far, my version of "running away" has been to stay home -- on Saturdays, the day when week in, week out, I'd drive 100 miles to visit my mom and my sister. Otherwise there is the "ER dump" strategy: you call 911 and tell the responders that he is suddenly not acting like himself and that he may have an infection but isn't cooperating with care. Do NOT mention cognitive impairment or dementia, as these are not medical emergencies and nothing can be done about it in the ER. 

Once he's there, ask to talk to the hospital social worker right away. Tell them he cannot come back into your home as you are not his caregiver and he no longer has a PoA and he is unsafe there. Some hospitals have been known to but impaired elders into taxis and send them back. You need to impress upon the discharge planner that you are unable to care for him, he is not cooperative with care and is an "unsafe discharge". Do not bring him back to your house no matter what the hospital promises or threatens. Give them the name and contact info and address for the PoA Uncle and let them harrass him instead. In some states they allow a Medicaid waiver that will pay for assisted living or memory care. Some facilities will accept the Medicaid waiver as full payment (in my experience these are not very nice places). In  other facilities they will accept it as full payment, but only if the resident has paid out of pocket for x number of years (2 usually). I had to provide bank statements, proof of income, cancelled checks, an explanation for what happened to her car, documents for the prepaid funeral, and explanation for large money transfers…. It’s a real process. I now pay the nursing home all but $50 (this is an allowance for personal needs, it also varies by state) of her income each month and Medicaid pays the rest. No government agency stepped in and made decisions about were mom went. As DPOA it was on me to make it all happen. I would definitely talk with an elder law attorney. There are income restrictions you might want to ask about, our lawyer suggested a prepaid funeral so family was not left with that expense, some assets will need to be sold, others they may need to keep(if it makes sense). Hi and welcome. I am sorry for your reason to be here but pleased you found this place.

There is no "reteach" for PWD. Learning requires both working and short-term memory which are impacted fairly early in the disease.

Emotional intelligence remains intact well into the later progression of the disease which means even "gentle correction" will come with feelings she will feel acutely. 

Many PWD have anosognosia and are unable to perceive their own areas of impairment. In your wife's mind, she the high functioning and capable woman she's always been even if she does admit to problems with her memory. 

The best practice around this sort of thing is to accept that you can't change her or her disabilities— only how you react to them. I found this short read helpful in reframing these kinds of issues.

=== COMMENT 1 (2026-10-29T20:18:29+00:00) ===
My parents’ hospice evaluation was done by a hospice intake nurse in their assisted living apartment.  Basically it’s a check of all their vitals - blood pressure, oxygen, heart rate, weight etc.  They basically check their balance, mobility, physical condition, medical history, medications, etc.  They will ask a series of questions about how well they can/can’t take care of themselves, their activities of daily living, what their diagnoses are.  They will contact their doctor, and then send all the information to the hospice doctor - who will decide if they are eligible for hospice. 

My step-dad was accepted on the first try.  He had been losing weight, had thyroid cancer nodules in his lungs, etc.  I did not attend that evaluation because he would have said no if I had said yes to any question.  The assisted living nurse attended along with my mom( although she had dementia). 

When mom was evaluated a few months later, she was denied the first time because she wasn’t losing height and was still able to do some of her ADLs even with dementia. The assisted living resident assistant that attended did not answer the questions about needing help correctly.  Two months later, the hospice agency called to schedule a re-evaluation.  I asked a different resident assistant to attend… and she answered the questions correctly.  Mom needed help showering, picking out clothes and dressing.  I knew she was incontinent.   She was also on oxygen for COPD. 

Something to keep in mind, dementia  patients have different eligibility criteria than those people with physical illnesses.  Mom was not expected to die soon when she was accepted.

I agree with everything @[member] says. In my sister's case, she was accepted by hospice during their first check - she had lost about 50lbs in about 4 months. 

Here's what wikipedia says about the difference between palliative care and hospice care in the US: 
Palliative care versus hospice care
See also: Hospice and palliative medicine and Hospice care in the United States

The distinction between palliative care and hospice differs depending on the global context. In the United States, the term hospice refers specifically to a benefit provided by the federal government since 1982. Hospice care services and palliative care programs share similar goals of mitigating unpleasant symptoms, controlling pain, optimizing comfort, and addressing psychological distress. Hospice care focuses on comfort and psychological support, and curative therapies are not pursued.[15] Under the Medicare Hospice Benefit, individuals certified by two physicians to have less than six months to live (assuming a typical course) have access to specialized hospice services through various insurance programs (Medicare, Medicaid, and most health maintenance organizations and private insurers). An individual's hospice benefits are not revoked if that individual lives beyond six months. In the United States, to be eligible for hospice, patients usually forego treatments aimed at a cure, unless they are minors. This is to avoid concurrent care, where two different clinicians are billing for the same service. In 2016, a movement began to extend the reach of concurrent care to adults who were eligible for hospice but not yet emotionally prepared to forego curative treatments.[16]
